claims.text: Selective dealloying can produce three-dimensional noble-metal-based high-entropy-alloy nanoframeworks.
Selective dealloying removes less noble elements from a homogeneous precursor alloy.
Removing the less noble elements leaves a porous, noble-metal-enriched scaffold.
The resulting scaffold has enhanced catalytic properties.
The precursor is a homogeneous NM-HEA containing both noble and less noble metallic elements.
Controlled chemical dealloying selectively dissolves the less noble elements.
Appropriate etchant, temperature, and duration can enable selective dissolution without structural collapse.
Appropriate dealloying conditions can preserve the desired atomic mixing.
Removal of less noble atoms forms a nanoporous, three-dimensional interconnected framework.
Preferential leaching of less noble components increases surface area.
Preferential leaching induces reorganization of the residual noble metals.
Reorganization of residual noble metals favors atomic-level proximity and potential strain effects.
Increased surface area, atomic-level proximity, and strain effects can expose additional catalytic sites and boost catalytic activity.
The dealloyed NM-HEA will have a well-defined three-dimensional porous structure.
The dealloyed NM-HEA will have a higher density of catalytically active sites than the precursor.
The dealloyed NM-HEA will exhibit improved catalytic performance relative to the precursor alloy.
The uniformly mixed precursor has lower accessible surface area for catalytic reactions than the proposed dealloyed material.
The method is limited to compositions in which less noble elements can be selectively removed without compromising structural integrity.
Atomic control and nanoporous architecture are sensitive to composition and dealloying conditions.
